name: oe-kimi-C-S-P
finalResponse:
Before you call it a transition, ask whether the revenue ever wished to be smooth.

You frame the trough as a problem to be modeled away—a cavity that competent management fills with forecasts and bridge financing. Consider instead that the lumpiness was the only honest thing your company ever said to the market. If you pave it, you do not achieve a business model; you achieve only a more sophisticated lie, told faster.

**On ownership, which must not be revoked**  
The perpetual license is not technical debt to be refinanced; it is a watershed. To announce a "migration path" is to tell your long-standing customers that the deed they hold was written in pencil, and that you have the eraser. Do not do this. Let the perpetual seat persist, but let it grow quiet. Stop selling upgrades to the holders; let their version fossilize with dignity, unbothered by telemetry or feature announcements. Build the subscription not as a replacement but as a neighboring country with its own passport and its own weather. If an existing customer wishes to cross, let them carry their history as an unpriced courtesy, not as a credit to be calculated by your finance team. The incentive to move is not a discount; it is the sudden, unofficial realization that their old license has become a relic—still honored, but no longer spoken of in the new rooms.

**On the subscription, which should arrive as a rumor**  
Do not call it a transition. Release the new offering without a funeral for the old. Price the subscription not against the license, but against the cost of your own obsolescence. For the first two years, bundle everything and unbundle nothing; let the value be so thick that the CFO cannot itemize it. Let the annual fee feel like membership in a society that has not yet published its rules. If you balance the trough by pulling adoption forward with aggressive discounts, you have merely disguised the old lumpiness in a new dress. Let the trough be deep. Let it be so deep that the investors can see the bottom and know you are not pretending. The depth is not a risk to mitigate; it is the only proof that the new model is breathing on its own.

**On the sales force, which must be paid for restraint**  
Discard the quota. The hero who closes the seven-figure upfront deal is worshipping a god who is about to die. Pay the rep not for extraction but for duration. Let the commission be a slow-release secret: half visible upon the subscription signature, half arriving only when the customer’s second renewal occurs without escalation, without intervention, without a hero. For the existing installed base, pay *nothing* for conversion. The rep who convinces a perpetual customer to subscribe should suspect, afterward, that the act was unnecessary—that the customer wandered in alone because the old country had gone silent. Let the large upfront deal remain technically possible but strategically unnamed, like a vintage wine available by request but absent from the menu. Salespeople cluster around what is measured; therefore, measure only patience.

**On the board, which must be told fables, not forecasts**  
Do not present a bridge with milestones. They have seen such bridges; they are the architecture of synchronized misunderstanding. Instead, report what has emerged without your direction. "In Q2, we observed that enterprise accounts with perpetual seats renewed maintenance at higher rates while shadow-purchasing subscription access outside any negotiated bundle." Let the board wonder if this is chaos or strategy. Do not volunteer which. When they ask the length of the trough, remind them that the competitor who lost a fifth of its base did so under surgical light, with every milestone met and every variance explained. Suggest that your ambiguity is the option premium paid for authentic transformation. If they demand a five-year model, give them a model with a door that opens onto a mist. The investor who needs every quarter explained has already calculated your failure into their portfolio theory. Keep only those directors who can tolerate not knowing.

You asked for a plan. I will offer you one:  

*Stop calling it a migration.* The installed base is not a population to be governed; they are proprietors of your previous truth. Let them remain perpetual. Let them sleep through your revenue recognition. In their silence and in the depth of your trough, the subscription model will either prove it has its own lungs, or it will reveal itself as a costume you have sewn to impress analysts. The only honest transition is the one you do not claim to control. Watch for the renewal that happens in year three without a call. Is it not possible that the customer who misunderstood your new pricing understood your value more clearly than the spreadsheet intended?
